openingMessage: What can I do about it now? That's the only question that matters when something isn't right. The moment you stop blaming, you gain control. That's where leadership begins.
openingWhy: Valve's weeping, the spotter didn't show, the wrong kill water got delivered — you can burn an hour on whose fault it is, or handle it and sort the story after. The leak doesn't pause for the argument. The hand asking 'what now' is running the job while everyone else runs the trial.
leadershipThought: Own the whole thing. Own your response. Own your equipment. Own your preparation. Own your outcome. That's what it means to be an Owl. Let's go to work.

specialFocus.title: Twelve Weeks, One Habit — Discipline Is What's Left
specialFocus.standardLabel: What I Carry Off This Program — Every Shift After Friday
specialFocus.why:
Twelve weeks ago we opened with Energy Isolation and a room full of people privately wondering how long this thing was going to last. Friday is the last one. So before anybody starts talking about what we covered, look at what this crew actually did.

In August alone: 548 completed OWL forms, 38 technicians, 412 locations. Stop work authority used 91 times. Unsafe conditions written up 118 times. Atmospheric hazards tested before the first break on 390 of them. And of the 392 forms that answered “did we leave it better than we found it” — 392 said yes. That last one is self-reported and I'll say so out loud. It is still 392 times somebody sat in the truck and asked himself the question before he drove off. Twelve weeks ago nobody was asking it.

Now here is the number that actually matters. The write-ups feeding our lessons library ran 195 in June, 169 in July, and 347 in August. Read that middle number again. July went down. That's the month the program stopped being new — and that is exactly where most safety programs quietly die. Ours didn't. August more than doubled July. The curve went up at the end, not the beginning. That is not enthusiasm. Enthusiasm is a June number. What you are looking at is discipline, and you built it yourselves.

So understand what Week 12 is. Work Authorization is not a thirteenth topic stacked on the other eleven — it is the one that holds them. Isolation, containment, line of fire, mobile equipment, confined space, driving, hot work, bypassing controls, excavation, lifting, height: every one of those is a control that only exists if somebody stops and authorizes the work before it starts. And out here the field never hands you one topic at a time. It hands you four at once, on a Tuesday, when you're already behind. Twelve weeks gave you twelve topics. Discipline is what makes all twelve available to you at the same time, on a location where nobody is watching.
standard: I do job 500 the way I did job 1. Familiarity is where shortcuts get born. The location I've been to forty times is the one that gets me, because it's the only one I stop looking at.

Nobody has to be watching. Twelve weeks of meetings end Friday. The gas, the pressure, the iron and the traffic do not. The only thing that carries past Friday is what I do when the board isn't up and nobody asked me for a form.
I don't get to pick the topic. The field doesn't run one week at a time. If I only sharpened up on whatever we talked about that Monday, I built nothing. All twelve or none.

I still write it down. A near-miss I keep to myself protects exactly one person — me, for about a day. A near-miss I write up protects 38 people for as long as we're out here. That's the whole reason the library exists.

I keep the standard when it costs me something. Anybody holds the line on an easy day. Discipline is the permit that isn't live yet, the walk-down nobody else wants to do, and the call I make when I know it's going to slow the job down.

scenarios.title: Week Thirteen
scenarios.body:
It's the first Monday after this program ends. There is no meeting. There is no board on the wall, no runsheet, no scenario, and nobody is going to read your name out for recognition. You get up at 4:00 the same as always and you drive to a location you've been to before. That morning is the entire program.

Everything up to Friday was practice with the lights on. Twelve weeks of somebody handing you the topic, reminding you what to look for, and asking you afterward how it went. Week thirteen is the first morning nobody hands you anything — and the exposure is exactly the same as it was in week one. The gas doesn't know the program ended.

So decide it now, in this room, not out there at 6:15 by yourself. What do you still do on September 7th? Do you still walk the location before you rig up? Do you still test before the first break? Do you still write the form when the job was clean and boring and nobody would ever know you skipped it? Because the honest answer is that a habit you only keep while somebody is checking was never a habit — it was compliance, and compliance ends when the checking does. The reason this program ran twelve weeks instead of one is that twelve weeks is roughly how long it takes for a thing to stop being something you remember to do and start being something you'd feel wrong not doing. If we got that right, week thirteen looks exactly like week twelve and none of you will even notice it happened.

So answer it here, not out there: what is the first thing you'd be tempted to let slide on a morning nobody is watching? Name it. That's the one you guard.

scenarios.title: The Tuesday That Doesn't Care Which Week It Is
scenarios.body:
You roll up mid-morning. Here is what's actually on that location: a workover rig is moving in, so there is mobile equipment in motion and a line of fire that changes every ten minutes. The job is a first break, so you have breaking containment and atmospheric monitoring. There's a man on the rig floor above where you'll be standing — working at height, except it's his height and your head. A vac truck is waiting on you, so somebody is already pushing on the clock. And the permit for the task you actually came to do has not gone live yet.

Count them. That is five of our twelve weeks, plus the one we're on, all standing in the same fifty feet of caliche at the same time. Nobody rang a bell and announced which topic Tuesday was going to be.

This is the part people miss about a twelve-week program. You didn't learn twelve things. You learned one thing twelve different ways. Stop. Look at what's actually in front of you, not what you expected to find. Confirm you're authorized to start. Make the call if you're not. The reason we spent a week on each of those topics was never so you could recite them — it was so that when four of them show up at once on a Tuesday you're already fluent in all four and you don't have to think about it. Discipline is what turns twelve separate lessons into one set of eyes.

questions: Twelve weeks in — which one of these topics actually changed how you work? Not which one was interesting. Which one made you do something different on a location.
Be straight with me: which week went in one ear and out the other? I'd rather know now than find out from an incident report, and it tells me what we run again.
In July our write-ups dropped before they came back up in August. What was different about July for you out in the field — and what pulled it back?
Have you written up a near-miss or an unsafe condition in the last twelve weeks? If not, is that because you didn't see one, or because you saw one and let it go?
Who in this crew got better over these twelve weeks in a way you noticed? Say their name right now — they probably don't know you saw it.
specialFocus.nonNegotiable: Twelve weeks built the habit. Friday ends the meetings, not the standard. Do job 500 the way you did job 1 — and do it on the mornings when nobody is checking, because those are the only ones that ever counted.
